prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The fourteen-year-old speaker feels overwhelmed by insecurities about her changing body, appearance, and social life.
- She is preoccupied with death and fears that she may not live to reach important milestones like graduation or adulthood.
- She feels burdened by responsibilities while lacking motivation or control over her life.
- She resents perceived unfairness, including being overlooked for the Math Team despite her stronger grades.
- Her mother’s repeated absence behind a closed bedroom door intensifies the speaker’s loneliness and lack of support.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

A fourteen-year-old voices the anxieties of adolescence through a rapid stream of worries about appearance, love, school, mortality, and an emotionally unavailable mother. The repeated image of her mother behind a closed bedroom door underscores the speaker’s isolation, showing how ordinary teenage fears become overwhelming without support.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: There, Nobody, Math

outputs.L1:
I am fourteen, and my skin has betrayed me.  
The boy I cannot live without still sucks his thumb in secret.  
Why are my knees always so ashy?  
What if I die before morning?  
And Momma’s in the bedroom with the door closed.

I have to learn to dance in time for the next party.  
My room is too small for me.  
Suppose I die before graduation—  
they will sing sad melodies, but finally tell the truth about me.  
There is nothing I want to do  
and too much that has to be done.  
And Momma’s in the bedroom with the door closed.

Nobody even stops to consider my side of it.  
I should have been on the Math Team;  
my marks were better than his.  
Why do I have to be the one wearing braces?  
I have nothing to wear tomorrow.  
Will I live long enough to grow up?  
And Momma’s in the bedroom with the door closed.

outputs.L3:
The fourteen-year-old speaker is overwhelmed by the pressures and uncertainties of adolescence. She feels deeply insecure about her changing body, her appearance, and her place in the social world around her. At the same time, she is preoccupied with death, worrying that she may not live long enough to experience major milestones such as graduation or adulthood. These fears make the future seem fragile and uncertain.

She also feels weighed down by responsibilities, even though she lacks the motivation and sense of control needed to manage them. Her frustration is intensified by what she sees as unfair treatment. For example, she resents being overlooked for the Math Team despite having stronger grades than those who were selected. This experience reinforces her sense that effort and ability are not always recognized.

Most painfully, the speaker lacks emotional support at home. Her mother is repeatedly absent behind a closed bedroom door, leaving the speaker to face her fears and frustrations alone. The closed door becomes a symbol of emotional distance, deepening her loneliness and making her feel abandoned at a time when she most needs reassurance and guidance.
outputs.L4:
At fourteen, the speaker experiences adolescence as a relentless flood of uncertainty. Her thoughts move rapidly from one fear to another: she worries about her appearance, whether she will ever be loved, how she is doing at school, and what the future might hold. Even questions about illness and death enter her mind. The speed and disorder of these anxieties reflect her emotional state. No single concern can be resolved before another takes its place, so ordinary teenage insecurities accumulate until they feel unbearable.

Beneath all these worries lies a deeper need for reassurance. The speaker wants guidance from her mother, but her mother remains emotionally unavailable, repeatedly shut away behind a closed bedroom door. That door becomes more than a physical barrier. It symbolizes the distance between mother and daughter and emphasizes the speaker’s sense that she must confront adolescence alone. Although the mother is nearby, she is inaccessible at the moment her daughter most needs comfort and understanding.

The contrast between the girl’s urgent inner monologue and her mother’s silence intensifies the loneliness of the text. Many of the speaker’s fears are common to adolescence, yet they seem enormous because she has no trusted adult with whom to share them. Her repeated focus on the closed door suggests both frustration and hope: she feels rejected, but she continues to seek her mother’s attention.

Ultimately, the text portrays adolescence not simply as a period of self-consciousness, but as a vulnerable stage in which emotional support is essential. The fourteen-year-old’s stream of worries reveals how concerns about beauty, love, school, and mortality can become overwhelming when they are faced in isolation. Through the recurring image of the mother behind the bedroom door, the text shows that the speaker’s greatest fear may not be any single problem she names, but the possibility that she will have to face them all alone.
outputs.L5:
### There Was Nobody Who Understood the Math

There was a small classroom at the end of the hallway where nobody ever went. On its blackboard, a single math problem had remained unsolved for years.

One afternoon, Lina entered the room and studied the strange symbols. At first, they seemed meaningless. Then she noticed a pattern: every number pointed toward another, like steps on an invisible staircase.

She worked until the sun disappeared. When she finally wrote the answer, the lights flickered and the old clock began ticking again.

“Is anybody there?” called a teacher from the hallway.

Lina smiled at the completed equation.

“Nobody,” she replied, “just math.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness prose poem from the perspective of a fourteen-year-old girl, blending insecurity, school pressures, crushes, fear of death, and family tension. Repeat the line “and momma’s in the bedroom with the door closed” as a refrain.
counterfactuals.output:
I am fourteen and my knees look wrong in every mirror, too knobby, too loud, like they enter the room before I do, and in algebra Mr. Bell says show your work but what if my work is just a swarm of crossed-out numbers, what if I am the crossed-out number, what if everyone else got a handbook in seventh grade explaining how to stand in hallways and laugh without checking who is watching—

and momma’s in the bedroom with the door closed

while the washing machine walks itself crooked across the floor and Dad rinses the same coffee cup three times, saying nothing, saying everything with the hard little click when he sets it in the sink, and I have a history test tomorrow on wars that ended but never really ended, dates marching into my skull with bayonets, 1914, 1939, remember, remember, remember or your whole life is ruined, according to the guidance counselor with the shiny red nails.

At lunch I peel the cheese off my pizza and watch Eli Harper push his hair out of his eyes and I hate him for having eyes and hair and hands, especially hands, and for asking if I understood question six, because now question six is sacred, now I want to fold it into a tiny square and keep it under my tongue, and then he laughs at something Mia says and my ribs become a cage in the bad way, in the way where the bird is stupid for hoping.

and momma’s in the bedroom with the door closed

and I wonder if she is crying or sleeping or staring at the ceiling where the old leak made a continent, and whether mothers can disappear while still being in the house, whether fathers can turn into weather, whether I will inherit the silence like her brown eyes or the little dent in her chin.

Sometimes at night I remember I will die. Not in a dramatic way, not violins, just I’ll be brushing my teeth and suddenly the mirror contains a skull, the stars are dead light, the toothpaste tastes like a hospital, and everyone I love is standing on a trapdoor they don’t know about. I want to run downstairs and make them promise not to, promise not to ever, but Dad is watching the blue television flicker and—

and momma’s in the bedroom with the door closed

so I text three dots to Eli and erase them, type hey and erase it, type do you ever feel like— and erase that too because feelings are embarrassing unless they fit inside a song, unless a pretty person sings them with perfect skin.

My science project is due Friday. My body is due every morning, unfinished. My future is due constantly. College, they say, career, potential, as if potential is not a piano suspended over my head by a fraying rope. I got a B-minus and Dad asked what happened, and I wanted to say everything, everything happened, the sun exploded five billion years from now, my best friend sat with someone else, my jeans pinched at the waist, Mom stopped humming in the kitchen, Eli’s shoulder touched mine for half a second by the lockers and I lived a whole life there—

and momma’s in the bedroom with the door closed

and maybe behind it she is only reading. Maybe she is painting her nails. Maybe she is building a small boat from blankets and breath. Maybe I am cruel for making her sadness about me, but everything is about me because I am fourteen, and nothing is about me because I am fourteen, because adults move around with locked faces and bills and passwords and say you’ll understand someday as if someday is a country I applied to and might not get into.

I press my ear to the door but don’t knock.

Down the hall my phone lights up.

hey, Eli writes, did you get six?

And my heart, ridiculous animal, begins again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental coming-of-age poem with almost no punctuation in which a teenage speaker worries about acne, ashy knees, braces, dancing, grades, clothes, graduation, and whether she will live to grow up.
counterfactuals.output:
in the bathroom mirror  
my face becomes a red constellation  
every star named tomorrow  

i rub lotion into my ashy knees  
until they shine like small moons  
still learning how to bend  

my braces hold a silver fence  
around all the words  
i am afraid to smile  

at the dance my body waits  
beside the speakers  
while everyone else becomes weather  

my grades arrive in black ink  
little doors marked  
good girl  
not enough  
try harder  

i wear the same jeans  
the same brave jacket  
the same borrowed idea of beautiful  

graduation hangs down the hallway  
a white gown floating without me  
a cap waiting to crown whoever i become  

some nights the future feels close  
as a dress zipped to my throat  

some nights it feels like a country  
that may not let me in  

i count my pimples  
my credits  
my breaths  

i practice my name  
with woman after it  

i practice being alive  
long enough to answer
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical monologue capturing the chaotic inner thoughts of an anxious Black adolescent girl whose mother has withdrawn behind a closed bedroom door.
counterfactuals.output:
Mama’s door has been closed for three hours, seventeen minutes, and maybe my whole life.

I know because the green numbers on the microwave keep changing their minds, and every time they do, I look up like the answer might be there. 8:42. 8:43. 8:44. Time walking around in socks, pretending not to make noise.

The door is white. Not clean white. Landlord white. Paint-over-everything white, with a brass knob that turns if you turn it, except I won’t. I already knocked twice.

First knock: soft.  
Mama?

Second knock: harder.  
You okay?

Nothing.

Not even the bed springs. Not even her church fan fluttering though church was Sunday and today is Thursday and why is that fan always on her nightstand like God might call roll at any moment?

I press my ear to the door.

The door says hush.

The refrigerator says hummmmmm.

The pipes cough in the walls.

A siren tears down our street, red light bleeding through the blinds, and for one stupid second I think it’s coming for us. For me. Because I forgot to wash the pot. Because I got a C on that algebra quiz. Because I rolled my eyes when Mama said fix my face and maybe my face stayed wrong too long.

I fix it now.

I stand in the hallway and arrange my mouth into sorry.

Mama, I’m sorry.

I don’t say it out loud. If I say it, then something has happened. If I say it, the whole house will hear how scared I am, and fear is nosy. Fear will invite cousins. Fear will bring folding chairs and aluminum pans. Fear will stand over the stove whispering, That poor baby, that poor baby.

I am not a baby.

I’m fourteen and five foot three and my hair is still half-done because Mama started the left side before she went quiet. Three twists swing neat beside my cheek. The rest rises around my head in a soft dark question.

At school, Nia said my hair looks like a storm cloud when I pick it out. She meant it nice. I think she meant it nice.

Maybe I am a storm cloud.

Maybe I have been carrying thunder into every room.

Mama came home with grocery bags cutting moons into her fingers. I should’ve helped faster. I should’ve seen her face. Grown girls are supposed to notice things. Black girls especially. Everybody says we’re grown before we get there—so why didn’t I know? Why didn’t my magical old-soul eyes catch the crack opening inside her?

She put the milk away.

She sat down.

She stood up.

She went to her room and shut the door like a period.

No—like a fist.

No—like a hand over a mouth.

I hate this door.

I love this door because she is behind it.

I hate that those can both be true.

My phone is warm in my palm. Auntie’s name waits on the screen. I could press call. I could say, Something’s wrong. But what if nothing is wrong? What if Mama is only sleeping? What if Auntie comes over loud and worried, and Mama opens the door with that look—the tired one, the Don’t put my business in the street look—and then I’m the dramatic girl again?

At school they call me dramatic when my voice gets sharp.

Aggressive when it gets loud.

Mature when they need me to swallow it.

So I swallow.

It sits in my throat, kicking.

Behind the door, something moves.

I stop breathing.

“Mama?”

My voice comes out small. I hate it for betraying me.

There—a sound. Maybe a sniff. Maybe a sheet dragged across a mattress. Maybe the house settling its bones.

I place my palm against the paint. On the other side, is she doing the same? Is her hand lined up with mine, brown skin to brown skin with a cheap white door between us?

“Mama,” I say, and this time I let my voice be what it is. Shaking. Young. Mine. “You don’t have to open it. Just—just knock, okay?”

The silence grows teeth.

“One knock if you hear me.”

I wait.

The microwave changes again.

The refrigerator hums.

A car laughs music into the night and carries it away.

Then—

knock.

So soft I could’ve dreamed it.

My knees fold before I tell them to. I sit on the hallway floor, back against the door, half my hair twisted, half reaching wild toward the ceiling.

“Okay,” I whisper.

Not because anything is okay.

Because she heard me.

Because I heard her.

Because sometimes okay is not a place you arrive. Sometimes it is only one small sound through a locked door, one knuckle against wood, saying:

I am still here.

I am still here.

I am still here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a three-paragraph prose poem about teenage angst. Use breathless run-on sentences, dark humor, ordinary school concerns, and recurring thoughts of dying young, ending each paragraph with the same image of Momma behind a closed door.
counterfactuals.output:
By first period I have already failed algebra, adulthood, and the impossible quiz called My Face in Fluorescent Lighting, and the hallways keep swallowing us in alphabetical order while my locker refuses to open like it knows I’ll die young and doesn’t see the point of giving back my gym shoes, which is fair, honestly, because Coach says run like your life depends on it and mine apparently depends on a mile I cannot finish without tasting pennies, so I laugh too loudly, borrow a pencil, write my name as if signing a confession, and picture the yearbook caption beneath my photograph: MOST LIKELY TO BECOME A CAUTIONARY ASSEMBLY, while the bell rings and rings and nobody answers, and at home there is Momma behind a closed door.

At lunch I trade my apple for three fries and a rumor, the cafeteria pizza shines like evidence, my best friend is crying in the bathroom because love has ended again before chemistry, and I tell her we are all temporary but in a funny voice so it counts as comfort, then we go dissect a frog whose calm dead face suggests it never had to choose electives or pretend not to care who left it on read, and I think maybe I’ll die young, tragically and photogenically, except my skin is breaking out and tragedy has standards, then the guidance counselor asks about my five-year plan and I say decomposition, she does not laugh, adults never recognize a joke when it wears black eyeliner, and waiting at the edge of everything is Momma behind a closed door.

By midnight homework breeds across the desk, essays mating with worksheets, tomorrow crouches in my backpack with its sharpened little teeth, and I scroll past everyone else’s perfect lives until my own feels like a typo, imagining dying young not as a wish exactly but as the chorus of a song stuck in my head, dramatic, embarrassing, impossible to turn off, while somewhere a college brochure promises I can become somebody for only forty thousand dollars a year, and I whisper that I am already somebody, unfortunately, then eat cereal from a mug because every bowl is dirty and every prophecy is hungry, and I listen for footsteps, for mercy, for morning, for Momma behind a closed door.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a confessional poem in the voice of a fourteen-year-old who feels overwhelmed by body changes, romance, academic unfairness, social expectations, and an emotionally unavailable parent. Make the voice intimate, urgent, and unpunctuated.
counterfactuals.output:
fourteen

my body keeps making decisions without me  
hips arriving like rumors  
my chest turning every hallway into a courtroom  
my skin shouting red secrets  
and everyone says this is normal  
like normal is supposed to feel less like drowning  

i like someone and it is terrible  
because one smile can ruin my whole afternoon  
because i practice saying hi in the bathroom mirror  
then pass them silent as a locked door  
because wanting to be seen  
and being seen  
are somehow the same nightmare  

today i studied until the numbers blurred  
and still got marked wrong  
while the boy beside me copied my work  
and got called brilliant  
the teacher said effort matters  
but i think effort only matters  
when the right person is making it  

everyone wants something from me  
be pretty but do not know it  
be smart but not annoying  
be funny but never loud  
be kind even when they are cruel  
be grateful  
be easy  
be less  

at home you ask how school was  
without looking up from your phone  
and i say fine  
because fine is the password  
that lets me leave the room  

sometimes i stand near you  
waiting for you to notice  
that i am becoming a person  
so fast it hurts  
that i need someone to tell me  
which parts are mine  
and which parts belong to everybody staring  

i am fourteen  
and every feeling has its hands around my throat  
every mirror has an opinion  
every grade feels like a sentence  
every silence from you grows teeth  

i do not need you to fix me  
i need you to look at me  
like i am not a problem waiting to happen  
like i am still your child  
like i am here  
like i am here  
like i am here
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
